doc_description: American Water Works Company, Inc. (NYSE: AWK) Form 10-K for the year ended December 31, 2020, detailing the nation’s largest publicly traded water/wastewater utility’s regulated and market-based operations, audited results (revenue $3.78B, net income $709M) with PwC ICFR attestation, COVID-19 impacts, a $22–$25B 10-year capex/portfolio plan, the announced sale of its New York subsidiary, and extensive California Monterey Peninsula/Carmel River regulatory and desalination permitting proceedings.

structure.title: Preface
structure.summary:
- SEC Form 10-K for American Water Works Company, Inc. (fiscal year ended December 31, 2020), including cover page details: Delaware incorporation; HQ at 1 Water Street, Camden, NJ; NYSE listing (ticker AWK); large accelerated filer; auditor attestation on internal control over financial reporting; not a shell company; aggregate market value ~$20.39B as of June 30, 2020; 181,439,255 shares outstanding as of February 19, 2021; proxy statement portions incorporated by reference into Part III.
- Full Table of Contents outlining Parts I–IV:
  - Part I: Business; Risk Factors; Unresolved Staff Comments; Properties; Legal Proceedings; Mine Safety Disclosures.
  - Part II: Market for Common Equity and Related Matters; Selected Financial Data; MD&A; Market Risk Disclosures; Financial Statements and Supplementary Data; Changes in and Disagreements with Accountants; Controls and Procedures; Other Information.
  - Part III: Directors and Executive Officers and Corporate Governance; Executive Compensation; Security Ownership and Related Stockholder Matters; Certain Relationships and Director Independence; Principal Accountant Fees and Services.
  - Part IV: Exhibits and Financial Statement Schedules; Exhibit Index; Signatures.
- Forward-Looking Statements section:
  - Identifies statements made under the safe harbor provisions of the Securities Act, Exchange Act, and the Private Securities Litigation Reform Act; lists common forward-looking terminology.
  - Topics covered include: future financial performance, liquidity, and cash flows; rate/revenue adjustments and regulatory filings (including addressing regulatory lag); growth and portfolio optimization (acquisitions/dispositions), including sale of the New York subsidiary; California water supply alternatives to Carmel River diversions; capital expenditure plans and funding; debt repayment/refinancing; execution of business and operational strategies; access to capital markets; outcomes and impacts of governmental/regulatory proceedings and potential sanctions; technology and strategic initiatives; COVID-19 impacts; utility privatization opportunities; industry and operational trends; regulatory, legislative, legal, and tax developments.
  - Caution that actual results may differ due to risks and uncertainties, highlighting factors such as:
    - Regulatory and governmental decisions (rates, capital structure, ROE, capex, acquisitions/dispositions, taxes, permitting, water supply/management), including COVID-19 responses and timeliness of actions.
    - Changes in customer demand and usage patterns (conservation, COVID-19).
    - Limits on water supply due to allocation rights, regulations, drought, or overuse.
    - Loss of large industrial/commercial customers from economic conditions or COVID-19.
    - Changes in laws and policies (environmental, health and safety, consumer/data privacy, water quality/accountability, emerging contaminants, public utility and tax rules) and impacts from elections/administration changes.
    - Weather, climate variability, and natural disasters (drought, abnormal rainfall, freezing, winds, flooding, pandemics, earthquakes, landslides, hurricanes, tornadoes, wildfires, storms, sinkholes, solar flares).
    - Litigation and governmental proceedings.
    - Risks from aging infrastructure and the ability to maintain, replace, and improve resiliency of systems and technology.

- Company overview (Item 1—Business): American Water, with roots back to 1886 and incorporated in Delaware in 1936, is the largest and most geographically diverse publicly traded U.S. water and wastewater utility by operating revenue and population served. It employs ~7,000 people, serving over 15 million people in 46 states.

- Business structure: The Company operates primarily through:
  - Regulated Businesses (its core utilities providing water and wastewater services subject to state PUC and environmental/health/water-quality regulation).
  - Market-Based Businesses (complementary services that collectively do not constitute a GAAP reportable segment).

- Definitions: References to “we,” “us,” “our,” “the Company,” and “American Water” mean American Water Works Company, Inc. and its subsidiaries; “parent company” refers to the standalone holding company.

- Regulated Businesses footprint and regulation: Utilities operate in 1,700+ communities across 16 states, with ~3.5 million active customer connections across residential, commercial, industrial, public authority, fire service, and resale categories. - Financial contribution of Regulated Businesses: Operating revenues were $3,255 million in 2020, $3,094 million in 2019, and $2,984 million in 2018, representing 86%, 86%, and 87% of total Company operating revenues, respectively.

- 2020 geographic mix and customer base: The “Top Seven States” by regulated operating revenue—New Jersey, Pennsylvania, Missouri, Illinois, California, Indiana, and West Virginia—collectively provided 87.7% of regulated operating revenue and 85.5% of regulated customers in 2020. Remaining “Other” states include Georgia, Hawaii, Iowa, Kentucky, Maryland, Michigan, New York, Tennessee, and Virginia.

- Notable forward-looking operational items: References to portfolio optimization and growth strategies, timing and outcomes of acquisitions, the announced sale of the New York subsidiary, California supply alternatives to Carmel River diversions, and ongoing technology and strategic initiatives.

structure.summary:
- Company overview: American Water is the largest publicly traded U.S. water and wastewater utility, with roots to 1886, ~7,000 employees, serving 15+ million people across 46 states. Operations are reported as Regulated Businesses (primary) and Market-Based Businesses (non-GAAP segment aggregation).

- Regulated Businesses:
  - Services and footprint: Water and wastewater utility operations in 1,700+ communities across 16 states, 3.5 million active customer connections; subject to state PUC regulation and environmental/health standards.
  - Revenues and customers: 2020 regulated revenues of $3.255B (86% of total). Top revenue states include NJ, PA, MO, IL, CA, IN, WV. Customer mix detailed by residential, commercial, fire service, industrial, public/other.
  - Metering/billing: Predominantly metered water customers; wastewater billed flat-rate or based on water use.
  - Growth drivers: System acquisitions, population growth within service areas, and bulk/wholesale sales.
  - Capital plan: $22–$25B over 10 years (including acquisitions), prioritizing main replacement, treatment/storage upgrades, resiliency, water quality, technology, and regulatory compliance. Pipe renewal cycle improved from 250-year (2009) to expected 110-year by 2025; ~2,200 miles planned for 2021–2025. Examples of resiliency projects in NJ and IN.
  - Regulation and ratemaking: Describes mechanisms to mitigate regulatory lag—e.g., infrastructure surcharges, future/hybrid test years, utility plant recovery, expense and revenue stability mechanisms, consolidated tariffs, deferred accounting—by state adoption.
  - M&A strategy: Focus on proximate acquisitions to existing footprint, with emphasis on wastewater consolidation; evaluates new markets for regulatory support and returns. Notes widespread municipal ownership of U.S. systems and drivers for privatization.
  - Notable transaction: Agreement to sell New York American Water to Liberty Utilities for ~$608M cash (subject to approvals and conditions), alongside NY state municipalization study activity.
  - Industry legislation: NJ Water Quality Accountability Act; fair market value statutes in multiple states; 2020 Indiana and West Virginia laws expanding valuation/recovery tools; federal COVID-19 relief funds for water assistance and SRF capitalization.
  - Competition: Limited direct competition in existing CPCN territories; competitive landscape for acquisitions includes large investor-owned utilities and infrastructure/energy firms.
  - Condemnation/eminent domain: Ongoing proceedings/risks, including Monterey, CA Measure J effort to acquire the Monterey system (environmental review, LAFCO steps, litigation) and an Illinois pipeline condemnation case by a regional water agency.
  - Water supply and wastewater services: Describes ownership of infrastructure (not water rights), sources (surface, groundwater, purchased), and state-specific source mix; addresses supply planning, drought and environmental constraints, and the Monterey Peninsula Water Supply Project (desalination and GWR purchases).
  - Seasonality: Higher third-quarter demand; revenue stability mechanisms in CA, IL, NY reduce weather-related variability.

- Market-Based Businesses:
  - Revenue contribution: ~$540M in 2020 (14% of total).
  - Homeowner Services Group (HOS): Warranty and home services (water/sewer line, gas/electric, HVAC, appliances, surge protection) via partnerships; ~3 million customer contracts in 43 states.
  - Military Services Group (MSG): 17 military installations under 50-year contracts; O&M plus capital replacement/expansion programs; evolving requirements for contractor financing on discrete projects; ~$6.2B revenue backlog with ~41 years average remaining; price redetermination/EPA mechanisms and termination provisions.
  - Contract Services Group (CSG): Five O&M contracts with municipalities.
  - Competition: HOS competes with HomeServe and Cinch; MSG with American States Water, Suez, Veolia.

- Environmental, health and safety, and water quality regulation:
  - Framework: Compliance with SDWA, Clean Water Act, LCR, CERCLA, and state rules (including earlier PFAS standards in NJ).
  - Investment and compliance: Estimated $725M over five years for environmental control facilities (including $155M in 2021); expected regulatory cost recovery through ratemaking.
  - SDWA specifics: Monitoring/standards for 90+ contaminants; Long-Term 2 and Stage 2 DBP rules; UV disinfection and other upgrades at ~30 surface plants (estimated $150–$250M remaining); extensive testing and industry recognition via EPA Partnership for Safe Water.
  - Lead and Copper Rule: EPA finalized Revised LCR (Jan 2021) with compliance by Jan 2024; company estimates <5% of service lines contain lead; plans to replace a significant majority of known LSLs by 2030 at an estimated $600M–$1.2B, favoring full external LSL replacement.
  - Clean Water Act/NPDES: Permitting and discharge compliance for wastewater; occasional violations/fines not expected to be material.

- Research & Development:
  - Focus areas: Contaminants of emerging concern (COVID-19 in wastewater, PFAS, Legionella, cyanotoxins, pathogens), disinfection byproducts, source-water monitoring, analytics, and treatment technologies (activated carbon, biofiltration, ion exchange).
  - Collaboration: Active engagement with EPA, CDC, state agencies, and research foundations; two laboratory facilities support R&D and quality control.

- Service Company and security:
  - Centralized shared services (finance, legal, engineering, operations, R&D, customer care centers, etc.) provided at cost to affiliates.
  - Security program: Physical, cyber, and OT security governance; periodic risk assessments; partnerships with law enforcement.

- ESG initiatives and performance:
  - Environmental: GHG reduction goal >40% by 2025 vs. 2007; 32% achieved through 2019. Water efficiency goal: 15% reduction per customer by 2035 (4.3% through 2020). Utility Resilience Index target +10% by 2030. >$700M planned resiliency capex (~8% of five-year plan).
  - Social: Safety leadership (2020 best ORIR at 0.99; 100k+ hours safety training; expanded near-miss reporting), high customer satisfaction, and significant charitable giving (including COVID-19 relief).
  - Governance: Independent, diverse board with relevant expertise; strong committee leadership and moderate tenure. External recognitions (FTSE4Good, MSCI ESG Leaders, Bloomberg GEI, Corporate Knights Global 100).

- Human capital resources:
  - Safety culture with “Stop Work Authority,” extensive training, and improving safety indicators.
  - COVID-19 response: No layoffs; enhanced benefits, leave, PPE, protocols, and flexibility.
  - Inclusion & diversity: Leadership roles established, partnerships with external organizations, training, and measurable hiring/promotion diversity; formation of I&D councils and ERGs.
  - Talent development: Minimum 20 training hours per employee; >350k hours in 2020; succession planning and internal mobility.
  - Workforce data: ~7,000 employees; 45% union-represented across 72 CBAs; 7.4% turnover; ongoing/anticipated negotiations.

- Executive leadership: Roster and roles of executive officers as of February 24, 2021, including CEO, CFO, COO (effective March 1, 2021), Presidents of Regulated Operations/MSG and Eastern Division, CHRO, General Counsel, CTO, Growth Officer, Controller, Treasurer, and Operational Excellence/Safety leader.

- Investor information: SEC filing access and corporate governance documents available via company website and investor relations portal (web content not incorporated by reference).

- Risk factors (beginning):
  - Regulatory risk: Dependence on PUC approvals for rates and operations; potential for disallowances, lag, penalties; COVID-19-related delays and emergency actions.
  - Environmental and water quality compliance risk: Costs and liabilities from evolving standards (including emerging contaminants), potential reputational impacts.

structure.title: Risk Factors
structure.heading: Item 1A. Risk Factors
structure.start_phrase:
We
 operate in a market and regulatory environment that involves significant risks, many of which are beyond our control.
structure.summary:
- Document type and scope: Excerpts from a Form 10-K covering Item 1A (Risk Factors), Item 1B (Unresolved Staff Comments), Item 2 (Properties), and part of Item 3 (Legal Proceedings).

- Regulatory environment and rate-setting:
  - Extensive regulation by state public utility commissions (PUCs) governs rates, financing, acquisitions, and operations; potential for fines and sanctions.
  - Rate case outcomes, timing, and “regulatory lag” can prevent timely recovery of costs and authorized returns; partial mitigations include revenue stability mechanisms, infrastructure surcharges, and future test years in some states.
  - COVID-19 has disrupted PUC processes and imposed moratoriums on shutoffs, creating uncertainty in approvals and collections.
  - Changing laws and policies (tax, environmental, data privacy such as CCPA) may increase costs, constrain operations, and affect recoverability in rates.

- Environmental, water quality, and wastewater risks:
  - Compliance obligations under CERCLA, Clean Water Act, Safe Drinking Water Act, Lead and Copper Rule, and state requirements; potential for significant O&M and capital costs, fines, and reputational harm.
  - Emerging contaminants (e.g., PFAS, pharmaceuticals, pathogens) may lack clear standards; detection/mitigation challenges and potential disallowance of cost recovery.
  - Wastewater system failures/overflows can cause environmental damage and liabilities, especially during heavy rainfall or flooding.

- Water supply and climate-related risks:
  - Dependence on publicly controlled sources, allocation rights, and purchase agreements; threats from drought, overuse, contamination, and endangered species protections.
  - Specific Monterey County, CA exposure: SWRCB orders (2009 and 2016) to reduce Carmel River diversions, a 2021 deadline, and potential fines/penalties if unmet.
  - Climate variability may increase droughts, storms, flooding, sea-level impacts, water quality degradation, and service disruptions; recovery in rates is uncertain.
  - Government-imposed conservation and use restrictions can reduce demand; demand reductions may persist post-drought.

- Operational reliability, infrastructure, and seasonality:
  - Severe weather, natural disasters, and pandemics can disrupt service and require significant repairs; cost recovery may be limited.
  - Aging infrastructure (mains, plants, dams) raises failure risk, O&M and capex needs, and potential for property/environmental damage.
  - Seasonality affects volumes and revenues; some states use revenue stability mechanisms to mitigate sales variability.

- Contamination and liability exposure:
  - Potential contamination of sources or delivered water from natural/man-made causes; may require service interruptions, “Do Not Use” orders, costly treatment, and could lead to litigation and enforcement actions.
  - Insurance and tariff protections may be limited; reputation risks even absent fault.

- Dams, pipelines, and reservoirs:
  - Ownership of numerous dams (mostly earthen) and extensive pipe/reservoir networks entails risk of failure, injuries, property damage, supply interruptions, and uninsured losses; regulators may require costly upgrades or decommissioning, with uncertain rate recovery.

- Growth strategy and acquisition risks:
  - Competition for system acquisitions from utilities, governments, and financial buyers; risks include integration challenges, undisclosed liabilities, capital needs, controls, and failure to realize synergies.
  - Eminent domain/condemnation threats from municipalities or private property owners (inverse condemnation) can force asset sales or compensation with risk of inadequate recovery; ongoing examples cited in CA (Monterey Measure J/MPWMD) and IL (pipeline case).

- Cybersecurity, data privacy, and technology:
  - Heightened risk of physical and cyber attacks on critical infrastructure; third-party/vendor vulnerabilities; potential for operational disruption, data breaches, litigation, regulatory penalties, and added security costs.
  - Growing privacy and data protection obligations (e.g., CCPA); noncompliance risks significant costs and reputational harm.
  - Reliance on technology systems (billing, operations, meters); failures (including meter performance issues) and challenges deploying/upgrading new tech can increase costs, disrupt operations, and affect controls and efficiency; recovery in rates not assured.

- Workforce, safety, and labor:
  - Inherently hazardous worksites and handling of chemicals; strict safety practices are critical; failures can cause injuries, fatalities, regulatory penalties, and reputational damage.
  - Significant unionized workforce with many CBAs subject to renewal; risk of work stoppages and higher labor costs.

- Financial, liquidity, and market risks:
  - High indebtedness and working capital deficit pose constraints; exposure to interest rate risk and refinancing needs; reliance on commercial paper, revolving credit, and term loans.
  - Market disruptions (including COVID-19), credit rating changes, or covenant breaches (e.g., debt-to-capitalization limits) can limit access to capital and increase costs; may necessitate cash conservation or reduced capex/dividends.
  - Use of derivatives may introduce mark-to-market volatility.
  - Holding company depends on subsidiary dividends subject to regulatory and contractual constraints.
  - Net operating loss carryforwards (federal and state) may not be fully utilized; valuation allowances may affect earnings.
  - Goodwill ($1.5B) subject to impairment risk from market or operating changes.
  - Pension and postretirement obligations sensitive to asset performance, discount rates, and healthcare trends; increased funding needs may not be fully recoverable in rates.

- Market-Based Businesses (e.g., Military Services Group):
  - Parent guarantees and deposits backing performance obligations create potential financial exposure.
  - U.S. government contracts can be terminated for convenience or default; subject to price redeterminations and complex procurement/security compliance; adverse outcomes could affect earnings and cash flows.

- Accounting, controls, and talent:
  - New or revised accounting standards could materially affect reported results and financial position.
  - Risks of undetected control/reporting errors despite SOX controls could lead to disallowance of cost recovery and harm reputation or market access.
  - Talent attraction/retention and succession planning are critical; shortages could impair operations.

- Properties (Item 2) overview:
  - Extensive asset base across U.S.: ~79 surface water plants, 530 groundwater plants, 150 wastewater plants, ~53,200 miles of mains/pipes, ~1,100 wells, ~1,600 pumping stations, ~1,300 treated water storage facilities, and 75 dams.
  - Significant ongoing infrastructure renewal programs; substantial property concentration in NJ and PA.
  - Property insurance maintained with deductibles/limits.

- Legal proceedings (Item 3 excerpt):
  - Focus on compliance with SWRCB orders requiring significant reductions in Carmel River diversions by Cal Am, efforts to secure alternative supplies, and potential penalties for noncompliance.

- Item 1B—Unresolved Staff Comments: None.

- Item 2—Properties:
  - Core assets include water and wastewater treatment plants; transmission, distribution and collection mains and pipes; wells and reservoirs; pumping stations; meters and hydrants; buildings, dams and treated-water storage; land/easements; vehicles; software rights; and other operational equipment.
  - Substantially all properties are held by subsidiaries, many subject to mortgage bond liens; the corporate HQ (Camden, NJ) is owned by a wholly owned subsidiary, and office space/equipment are leased within the subsidiary structure.
  - Regulated Businesses asset scale (approximate): 79 surface water treatment plants; 530 groundwater treatment plants; 150 wastewater treatment plants; 53,200 miles of mains/pipes; 1,100 groundwater wells; 1,600 pumping stations; 1,300 treated-water storage facilities; 75 dams.
  - Ongoing system renewal across all states includes rehabilitation and replacement of aging or damaged mains/equipment.
  - Market-Based Businesses mainly hold office furniture and IT equipment.
  - About 52% of all properties are in New Jersey and Pennsylvania.
  - Property insurance maintained; the company is self-insured for deductibles and losses above coverage; assets are maintained to industry standards.

- Item 3—Legal Proceedings:
  - California—Carmel River Diversions and Monterey Peninsula Water Supply Project (MPWSP):
    - SWRCB 2009 Order and 2016 Order require substantial reductions in Carmel River diversions and impose milestones tied to MPWSP progress; missed milestones can trigger up to 1,000 acre-feet/year diversion reductions (one such reduction was imposed for 2020 milestones).
    - Conflicting interpretations between SWRCB and MPWMD over baseline/increased-use calculations; Cal Am pursued declaratory relief and engaged with agencies to reconcile guidance.
    - Petition to add alternative milestones based on Pure Water Monterey expansion was dismissed without prejudice (Dec 2019); Cal Am questions sufficiency/reliability of the alternative supply.
    - CPUC approvals: 2016 decision authorized a GWR water purchase agreement and related pipeline/pump stations with recovery of up to $50 million plus AFUDC; 2018 decision granted a CPCN for MPWSP, affirmed it as the preferred solution, and adopted a $279 million project cost (plus AFUDC), with cost recovery subject to prudence review after operations commence. As of Dec 31, 2020, Cal Am has incurred $154 million (including $36 million AFUDC) and cannot assure full cost recovery beyond previously approved amounts.
    - GWR water purchase agreement defaults: Agencies missed initial delivery (July 2019) and Performance Start Date (Jan 1, 2020); Cal Am reserved termination rights but did not terminate; Agencies later set Sept 1, 2020 as Performance Start Date; compliance to be assessed after June 30, 2021.
    - WRAMP False Claims Act suit regarding MPWSP environmental analysis was dismissed; appeal later dismissed in exchange for cost waiver.
    - Coastal permitting: City of Marina denied a coastal development permit; Cal Am appealed to the Coastal Commission and also filed an original jurisdiction application. Coastal Commission staff twice recommended denial citing environmental/resource impacts and an allegedly feasible alternative; Cal Am withdrew and refiled its application to address environmental justice issues; the Commission requested additional information (notice of incomplete application issued Dec 3, 2020).
    - Monterey County combined development permit for the desalination plant was approved (2019); MCWD litigation led to a court decision (Jan 2021) setting aside the approval for limited noncompliance while denying most other claims and lifting a prior construction stay.
    - City of Marina proposed zoning and local coastal plan changes to restrict the CEMEX site (intake/slant wells) advanced at the city level and await Coastal Commission approval.
    - Test slant well permits: Coastal development permits approved; amendments allow the well to remain and be maintained until Feb 28, 2022; state lands lease expires Dec 16, 2022; pumping ceased in Feb 2018 except minimal maintenance.
    - Land rights at CEMEX site: A permanent easement for intake wells was recorded (June 2018). The City contests the easement and seeks to limit extractions and exports under a 1996 annexation agreement; lawsuits filed against Cal Am and CEMEX, with various demurrers largely overruled; MCWD cross-complaint narrowed (nuisance claim dismissed without leave).
    - SGMA governance: Overlapping GSA claims (SVBGSA, City of Marina) at the CEMEX site led to the County of Monterey being accepted as exclusive GSA (Dec 2019); the City sued to challenge the County’s designation; Cal Am intervened. Cal Am also filed a validation action against the City’s GSP for the site; that action is stayed pending the City’s suit.

- Scope and purpose: Management’s Discussion and Analysis and Market Risk disclosures from American Water’s Form 10-K, including forward-looking statements and references to prior-year MD&A.
- Company overview: Largest publicly traded U.S. water and wastewater utility; ~7,000 employees serving 15+ million people; two segments—Regulated Businesses (PUC-regulated utilities in 16 states, ~3.5 million active customers) and Market-Based Businesses (not PUC rate-regulated).

Regulatory responses include deferred accounting authorizations in 11 of 14 jurisdictions (as of Feb. 24, 2021), cost recovery mechanisms in CA and IL; recorded ~$30 million regulatory assets and ~$4 million regulatory liabilities; disconnection moratoria status varies by state.
- 2020 financing actions: Established a 364-day term loan facility up to $750 million; drew $500 million in March 2020. AWCC issued $1.0 billion in senior notes (2.80% due 2030; 3.45% due 2050). Refinanced higher-cost debt with ~$311 million in lower-rate private activity/government-funded bonds.

- Growth strategy and 2020 activity: Invested ~$1.9 billion, including ~$1.8 billion in regulated capex and ~$135 million for acquisitions adding ~37,800 customers; ~14,500 customers added organically. Early 2021 closed two small acquisitions (~600 customers) and had agreements pending for ~30,000 additional customers.
- NY subsidiary divestiture: Agreement to sell New York American Water to Liberty for ~$608 million cash; assets/liabilities classified as held for sale.
- Market-Based Businesses growth: MSG awarded 50-year contract for Joint Base Lewis-McChord (estimated ~$771 million revenue, subject to annual adjustment).
- Long-term investment plan: Expect $10.3–$10.5 billion (2021–2025) and $22–$25 billion (2021–2030), including ~$1.9 billion in 2021; plan allocates ~$8.9 billion over five years to regulated infrastructure and $1.4–$1.6 billion to regulated acquisitions.
- Operational efficiency: Adjusted regulated O&M efficiency ratio improved to 34.3% (non-GAAP), with reconciliation provided and limitations discussed.
- Regulatory matters—rates and surcharges: Summaries of general rate case outcomes (2018–2020) with notable increases in NJ, IN, CA, and prior-period awards in PA, MO, WV, KY, NY, MD, VA; pending cases in IA, MO, PA, and CA (including cost of capital timing). Infrastructure surcharge (DSIC/WWISC) authorizations increased annualized revenues; additional 2021 surcharges approved and filings pending.
- Tax and legislative updates: CARES Act had no material impact; TCJA EADIT treatment described (returns to customers, timing by jurisdiction); federal NOL carryover of ~$366 million expected to be fully utilized in 2021; multiple state legislative changes facilitating fair value acquisitions, distressed system remedies, surcharge recoveries, cybersecurity programs, and rate mechanisms; CPUC low-income program decision impacts future California WRAM design.
- Consolidated and segment results: 2020 consolidated revenues $3.777 billion; Regulated Businesses revenues $3.255 billion with growth from rate increases, acquisitions/organic growth, and weather; residential volumes rose, C&I declined; EADIT reduced other revenues. Detailed O&M components (employee costs, purchased water, supplies/services, maintenance, insurance), D&A increases (offset by NY held-for-sale), and pension/OPEB non-service cost improvements.
- Market-Based Businesses performance: Revenues roughly flat year-over-year; MSG growth (capital upgrades, military contracts); HOS growth (pricing, contract expansion); offsets from Keystone divestiture and contract expirations; lower D&A post-divestiture; higher taxes on increased pre-tax income.
- Liquidity and capital resources: Capital-intensive model funded by operating cash flows, debt, and potentially equity; AWCC $2.25 billion revolving credit facility (to March 2025) supports $2.10 billion commercial paper and up to $150 million letters of credit; available liquidity at 12/31/20 was ~$1.935 billion; term loan $500 million outstanding at year-end. Plans to fund capex beyond operating cash flows through a mix of long-term debt and equity.
- Cash flows: 2020 operating cash flow ~$1.426 billion (benefiting from higher net income, lower hedge settlements; working capital headwinds from receivables, unbilled revenue, and payables timing); investing cash outflows driven by higher capex; financing inflows from debt issuance and term loan; higher dividends; no 2020 share repurchases.
- Debt management and hedging: Detailed 2020 issuances and retirements; treasury lock termination generated ~$6 million loss amortized to interest; universal shelf registration in place through May 2021.
- Capital structure and covenants: 12/31/20 capitalization ~37% equity, ~54% long-term debt, ~9% short-term debt/current maturities; debt-to-cap covenant limit 70% (actual ~63%); security ratings Baa1 (Moody’s) and A (S&P) with stable outlooks; discussion of AWCC support agreement and structural subordination considerations.
- Dividends and insurance: Notes dividend policy and regulatory constraints; describes insurance coverage scope and deductibles/limits.
- Critical accounting policies: Regulatory accounting (recognition and recoverability of regulatory assets/liabilities), income taxes (ASC 740, uncertain tax positions, EADIT), pension and OPEB (key assumptions, plan asset allocations, 2018 retiree medical plan changes and remeasurement), revenue recognition across Regulated, HOS, and MSG (including unbilled revenue), and contingencies.
- Market risk (Item 7A): Interest rate risk on variable/fixed debt and commercial paper (1% rate increase would add ~$6 million to short-term interest expense); commodity price risk (chemicals, power) mitigated via contracts and regulatory recovery; equity market volatility risk; credit risk management practices and diversified customer base, with regulated recovery mechanisms for uncollectibles.

Judgments consider case nature, applicable law, counsel input, and similar cases. Actual outcomes may differ and impact liabilities, revenue, and expenses. References to Note 17 (Commitments and Contingencies) and Note 2 (Significant Accounting Policies).
- New accounting standards: Referenced to Note 2 for recent standards.
- Market risk (Item 7A):
  - Interest rate risk: Exposure from variable and fixed-rate debt and commercial paper; managed by limiting variable exposure and using derivatives (e.g., swaps, swaptions, Treasury locks). A hypothetical 1% increase in rates would increase short-term interest expense by $6 million as of December 31, 2020.
  - Commodity price risk: Exposure to chemicals, electricity, and other inputs mitigated via contracts and expected regulatory recovery through rates; supplier non-performance could materially affect results and cash flows.
  - Equity price/stock volatility: Company’s share price may fluctuate due to market movements, industry events, analyst estimates, interest rates, and regulatory actions, potentially constraining future capital market access.
  - Credit risk: Arises from Regulated Businesses (serving residential, commercial, industrial, other customers) and Market-Based Businesses (developers, government entities, others). Managed via credit and collection policies, monitoring, and mitigants (letters of credit, prepayments). Portfolio is diversified with no significant concentrations; regulated operations generally recover prudently incurred uncollectible expenses through rates.
  - Retirement trust asset risk: Exposure to debt and equity markets and interest rates affecting pension/other benefits expense and funding. Risk mitigation via asset diversification and long-duration fixed income aligned with liability duration; expectation to recover benefit costs through rates.
  - Macroeconomic and regulatory risk: Economic downturns can affect customer receivables; uncertainty in regulatory rate authorizations may impact cost recovery, investment recovery, and returns in regulated operations.

nodes.title: Leases
nodes.heading: Leases
nodes.start_phrase: On January 1, 2019, the Company adopted Accounting Standards Update 2016-02, Leases (Topic 842), and all related amendments (collectively, the “Standard”).
nodes.summary:
- Lease accounting adoption: Company adopted ASC 842 (Topic 842) on January 1, 2019 using the modified retrospective approach and optional transition method, applying practical expedients (lease identification/classification, initial direct costs, hindsight, land easements). Prior periods not restated; cumulative-effect adjustment recorded to opening retained earnings.
- Recognition and impact: Recorded operating lease right-of-use (ROU) assets of ~$117 million and operating lease liabilities of ~$115 million at adoption; difference adjusted to retained earnings. No material impact on results of operations and no impact on cash flows.
- Lease portfolio and presentation: Company has operating and finance leases for real estate, utility assets, vehicles, and equipment. Operating leases presented as ROU assets, accrued liabilities, and operating lease liabilities; finance leases in PP&E, accrued liabilities, and other long-term liabilities. Policy election to exclude leases with terms of 12 months or less.
- Measurement and expense: ROU assets and liabilities recognized at commencement based on present value of lease payments using the incremental borrowing rate when no implicit rate is available; includes upfront payments and excludes incentives. Options to extend/terminate considered when reasonably certain. Lease expense recognized on a straight-line basis.
- Components and other terms: Lease and non-lease components generally accounted for separately, but combined for certain leases. Some leases include variable payments indexed to inflation. Portfolio approach applied to account for ROU assets and liabilities. No material residual value guarantees or restrictive covenants.
- Goodwill definition and allocation: Goodwill equals purchase price excess over fair value of net assets acquired; not amortized; allocated to reporting units. Company’s goodwill stems primarily from acquisitions in 2001 (E’town), 2003 (American Water by a prior owner’s affiliate), and 2018 (Pivotal). Regulated Businesses aggregated into one reporting unit; Market-Based Businesses include HOS and MSG reporting units.
- Impairment testing: Performed annually as of November 30 and when triggering events occur. Uses a qualitative assessment to determine need for quantitative testing. If necessary, a quantitative fair value test compares reporting unit fair value to carrying value; impairment recognized for the excess, limited to the amount of goodwill for that unit.

nodes.title: Goodwill
nodes.heading: Goodwill
nodes.start_phrase: Goodwill represents the excess of the purchase price paid over the estimated fair value of the assets acquired and liabilities assumed in the acquisition of a business.
nodes.summary:
- Leases: Adoption of ASC 842 on January 1, 2019 using the modified retrospective approach and optional transition method, with practical expedients applied. Recognition of operating lease right‑of‑use assets (~$117 million) and liabilities (~$115 million) at adoption; difference recorded to retained earnings. No material impact on results of operations or cash flows. Policies detailed for identifying leases; accounting presentation for operating and finance leases; exclusion of short‑term leases; measurement using incremental borrowing rate; treatment of lease and non‑lease components, variable payments, options, and portfolio approach; no material residual value guarantees or restrictive covenants.
- Goodwill: Definition, allocation to reporting units, and impairment testing framework. Goodwill primarily from acquisitions (American Water 2003, E’town 2001, Pivotal 2018). Annual impairment test as of November 30 with qualitative assessment first and quantitative DCF-based testing if needed. Reporting units: Regulated Businesses aggregated into one unit; Market-Based Businesses include HOS and MSG. Emphasis on management judgment and key assumptions; potential for material impact; cross-reference to Note 9.
- Intangible assets: Primarily finite‑lived customer relationships from Pivotal acquisition, initially measured at fair value and amortized over useful lives based on benefit pattern; cross-reference to Note 9.
- Impairment of long‑lived assets: Process for testing PPE, goodwill, intangibles, and long-term investments when indicators arise, using expected future cash flows and fair value comparisons; recognition of impairment losses. Regulated utilities tested on a separate entity basis; regulatory assets expensed if recovery no longer probable; estimation risks noted.
- Advances for construction and contributions in aid of construction: Description of customer/developer funding mechanisms for utility expansions. Advances refundable for limited periods (expected refunds: $23 million in 2020; $25 million in 2019). Non‑refundable advances reclassified to contributions, which reduce rate base. Typical practice of depreciating contributed plant and amortizing contributions as a reduction of depreciation expense, with some subsidiaries not amortizing per regulatory guidelines. Amortization amounts: $32 million (2020), $29 million (2019), $28 million (2018).
- Revenue recognition: Adoption of ASC 606 on January 1, 2018 using the modified retrospective approach applied to incomplete contracts.

nodes.title: Intangible Assets
nodes.heading: Intangible Assets
nodes.start_phrase: Intangible assets consist primarily of finite-lived customer relationships associated with the acquisition of Pivotal.
nodes.summary:
- Goodwill impairment testing: Requires significant management judgment to identify reporting units and estimate fair value via discounted cash flow analysis, using assumptions such as future operating results, discount rates, and growth rates. Deviations from assumptions could materially impact the consolidated financial statements. Referenced Note 9—Goodwill and Other Intangible Assets.
- Intangible assets: Primarily finite-lived customer relationships from the Pivotal acquisition, initially recorded at fair value and amortized over their useful lives based on the pattern of economic benefit. Referenced Note 9.
- Impairment of long-lived assets: Covers property, plant and equipment, goodwill, intangible assets, and long-term investments. Assets are tested when indicators suggest non-recoverability; fair value is estimated from expected future cash flows (including potential disposition) and compared to carrying value; losses recognized for any excess carrying value. For regulated utilities, assets are grouped on a separate-entity basis due to integrated statewide operations and uniform tariffs; regulatory assets are expensed if future recovery in rates is no longer probable. Notes the potential for material impact if assumptions differ from actual experience.
- Advances for construction and contributions in aid of construction: Regulated utilities may receive customer/developer funding to extend service. Advances are refundable for limited periods, with expected refunds recorded in other current liabilities ($23 million at 12/31/2020; $25 million at 12/31/2019). Nonrefundable advances are reclassified as contributions, which generally reduce rate base. Typically, utilities depreciate contributed plant and amortize contributions as a reduction to depreciation expense, though some subsidiaries do not amortize contributions. Amortization of contributions was $32 million (2020), $29 million (2019), and $28 million (2018).
- Revenue recognition: Adoption of ASC 606 effective January 1, 2018, using the modified retrospective approach applied to contracts not completed as of that date.

nodes.title: Impairment of Long-Lived Assets
nodes.heading: Impairment of Long-Lived Assets
nodes.start_phrase: Long-lived assets include property, plant and equipment, goodwill, intangible assets and long-term investments.
nodes.summary:
- Goodwill impairment testing: Management judgment in identifying reporting units and estimating fair value via discounted cash flow analyses; key assumptions include future operating forecasts, discount rates, and growth rates; potential for material impacts if assumptions differ; reference to Note 9—Goodwill and Other Intangible Assets.
- Intangible assets: Primarily finite-lived customer relationships from the Pivotal acquisition; initially recorded at fair value and amortized over useful lives based on the pattern of economic benefit; reference to Note 9.
- Impairment of long-lived assets: Covers property, plant and equipment, goodwill, intangible assets, and long-term investments; impairment testing when indicators arise, using expected future cash flows (and disposition, if applicable) to estimate fair value; recognize loss when carrying value exceeds fair value. For regulated utilities, assets are grouped on a separate entity basis due to integrated operations and uniform tariffs; regulatory assets are expensed if future recovery is no longer probable; potential material impacts if estimates change.
- Advances for construction and contributions in aid of construction (CIAC): Utilities receive advances/contributions from customers, builders, and developers to extend service; advances are refundable for limited periods as customers connect, with expected refunds recorded in other current liabilities ($23 million at December 31, 2020; $25 million at December 31, 2019); nonrefundable advances reclassified to contributions, which reduce rate base. Generally, the company depreciates contributed plant and amortizes contributions as a reduction to depreciation expense (some subsidiaries do not amortize and retain contributions on the balance sheet indefinitely). CIAC amortization was $32 million (2020), $29 million (2019), and $28 million (2018).
- Revenue recognition: Adoption of ASC 606 effective January 1, 2018 using the modified retrospective approach applied to contracts not completed as of that date.

nodes.title: Advances for Construction and Contributions in Aid of Construction
nodes.heading: Advances for Construction and Contributions in Aid of Construction

For regulated utilities, assets are tested on a separate-entity basis given integrated, statewide operations and uniform tariffs; regulatory assets are expensed if future recovery in rates is no longer probable. Assumption changes could materially impact results.

The Company typically depreciates plant funded by contributions and amortizes the contributions balance as a reduction of depreciation expense, though some subsidiaries, per regulatory guidelines, do not amortize contributions. Amortization of contributions was $32 million (2020), $29 million (2019), and $28 million (2018).

nodes.title: Revenue Recognition
nodes.heading: Revenue Recognition
nodes.start_phrase: On January 1, 2018, the Company adopted Accounting Standards Codification Topic 606, Revenue From Contracts With Customers, and all related amendments (collectively, “ASC 606”), using the modified retrospective approach, applied to contracts which were not completed as of January 1, 2018.
nodes.summary:
- Goodwill impairment testing: management judgment, discounted cash flow valuation, key assumptions (future operating results, discount and growth rates), potential material impacts, and reference to Note 9.

- Revenue recognition under ASC 606: adoption via modified retrospective on January 1, 2018; five-step model; performance obligations, transaction price allocation, and use of practical expedient for significant financing components due to short payment terms.
- Regulated businesses revenue: water and wastewater services treated as a single performance obligation recognized over time; inclusion of billed and unbilled revenues; recognition of probable recoveries/refunds through ratemaking.
- Market-based businesses revenue: home warranty/protection programs with separate performance obligations recognized ratably over time; handling of customer advances; long-term fixed-fee O&M contracts for U.S. government and municipal customers with ratable revenue recognition; separate capital improvement obligations recognized over time; treatment of contract losses, unbilled revenues, billings in excess, and estimate revisions.
- Income taxes: participation in a consolidated federal return with tax expense allocated as if subsidiaries filed separately.

nodes.title: Regulated Businesses Revenue
nodes.heading: Regulated Businesses Revenue
nodes.start_phrase: Revenue from the Company’s Regulated Businesses is generated primarily from water and wastewater services delivered to customers.
nodes.summary:
- Explains ASC 606 concepts, defining a performance obligation as a promise to transfer distinct goods or services (or a series) and recognizing revenue when control transfers, in amounts reflecting expected consideration.
- Outlines the ASC 606 five-step model: identify contracts; identify distinct performance obligations; determine the transaction price; allocate the price to obligations; recognize revenue when/as obligations are satisfied.
- Notes customer payment terms are generally within 30 days and do not exceed one year; the significant financing component practical expedient is applied.
- Regulated Businesses: Revenue primarily from water and wastewater services treated as a single performance obligation; recognized over time as services are provided; limited variable consideration and no significant financing components; includes cycle billings and unbilled revenues based on estimated usage; invoice amounts correspond to value transferred; revenue also recognized for probable recoveries/refunds via the ratemaking process.
- Market-Based Businesses (home warranty/protection programs): Fixed-fee services (e.g., water/sewer lines, HVAC, appliances, surge protection), typically one-year terms; each service is a separate performance obligation satisfied over time; revenue recognized ratably; payments monthly or annual; advances deferred until performance.
- Long-term O&M contracts for U.S. government and municipal customers: Fixed-fee revenue recognized ratably over the contract term; capital improvements initiated by contract modifications are treated as separate performance obligations with stand-alone fixed pricing; revenue recognized over time based on performance; unbilled revenues and billings in excess handled as assets/liabilities; losses recognized when probable and estimable; changes in estimates recorded when determined.
- Income taxes: The company files a consolidated federal return; group members are charged tax expense as if filing separate returns.

nodes.title: Market-Based Businesses Revenue
nodes.heading: Market-Based Businesses Revenue
nodes.start_phrase: Through various warranty protection programs and other home services, the Company provides fixed fee services to residential customers for interior and exterior water and sewer lines, interior electric and gas lines, heating and cooling systems, water heaters and other home appliances, as well as power surge protection and other related services.
nodes.summary:
- Explains ASC 606 revenue recognition, defining performance obligations and applying the five-step model: identify contracts, identify distinct performance obligations, determine transaction price, allocate price to obligations, and recognize revenue when/as obligations are satisfied.
- States that transaction price is allocated to distinct performance obligations and revenue reflects consideration expected; revenue is recognized when control transfers.
- Notes practical expedient for significant financing components: customer payments are generally due within 30 days and no payment terms exceed one year, so no financing component is recognized.
- Regulated Businesses:
  - Revenue primarily from water and wastewater services under contracts with a single, non-distinct performance obligation.
  - Revenue recognized over time as services are provided; generally no significant financing components or variable consideration.
  - Includes billed amounts and unbilled revenue estimated from last meter read to period end; right-to-invoice aligns with value transferred.
  - Recognizes amounts when probable of future recovery/refund through ratemaking.
- Market-Based Businesses:
  - Home warranty/protection programs (water/sewer lines, electric/gas lines, HVAC, water heaters, appliances, surge protection): fixed-fee, typically one-year term, each service is a separate performance obligation recognized ratably over time; customers pay monthly or annually; advances deferred until obligations are met.
  - Long-term fixed-fee operate-and-maintain contracts for U.S. government and municipal customers: revenue recognized ratably over contract term.
  - Capital improvements under these contracts are separate performance obligations created via contract modifications with stand-alone fixed pricing; revenue recognized over time based on performance completed.
  - Contract loss recognition when losses become probable and estimable.
  - Unbilled revenues recognized when performance exceeds billings; billings in excess recorded as liabilities; estimate changes to costs/revenues recognized in the period determined; references Note 5 for more detail.
- Income taxes: company and subsidiaries file a consolidated U.S. federal return; each member is charged tax expense as if filing separate returns.

nodes.title: Income Taxes
nodes.heading: Income Taxes
nodes.start_phrase: The Company and its subsidiaries participate in a consolidated federal income tax return for U.S. tax purposes.
nodes.summary:
- Describes the company’s revenue recognition under ASC 606, including the five-step model, identification of performance obligations, allocation of transaction price, and recognition upon transfer of control; applies the practical expedient for significant financing components because customer payment terms are under one year.
- Regulated Businesses revenue: generated from water and wastewater services with a single performance obligation; recognized over time as services are provided; includes billed and estimated unbilled usage; uses right-to-invoice as evidence that invoice amounts reflect value transferred; recognizes amounts tied to probable future recoveries/refunds through ratemaking.
- Market-Based Businesses revenue: fixed-fee home warranty/protection services (water/sewer lines, utilities, HVAC, appliances, surge protection) generally with one-year terms; each service is a separate performance obligation satisfied over time; revenue recognized ratably over the service period; customer advances deferred until performance.
- Long-term operations and maintenance contracts for U.S. government/military installations and municipal facilities: fixed fees recognized ratably over contract terms; capital improvements handled via separate contract modifications with standalone pricing and treated as separate performance obligations recognized over time; recognizes contract losses when probable and estimable; manages unbilled revenue and billings in excess; reflects revisions to estimates in the period determined.
- Income taxes: files a consolidated federal return; members charged as if filing separately; records deferred taxes for temporary differences using enacted rates; regulated utilities record regulatory assets/liabilities for tax effects expected to be realized through rates; investment tax credits deferred and amortized over asset lives; interest and penalties on tax positions recorded in income tax expense; sales taxes reported on a net basis.
- Allowance for Funds Used During Construction (AFUDC): non-cash credit to income with corresponding addition to utility plant; borrowed-funds portion reduces interest expense, equity portion recorded in other income; amounts reported (in millions): Allowance for other funds used during construction—$30 (2020), $28 (2019), $24 (2018); Allowance for borrowed funds—$13 (2020), $13 (2019), $13 (2018).
- Environmental costs: complies with environmental regulations; expenses or capitalizes current-benefit costs and accrues undiscounted remediation costs when probable and estimable; notes a conservation agreement (NOAA) requiring $1 million annual payments from 2010 through 2021 to protect steelhead trout habitat in California’s Carmel River; remediation accruals of $1 million (2020) and $2 million (2019).
- Derivative financial instruments: used solely to hedge interest rate risk; no speculative or leveraged positions; all derivatives recorded at fair value; fair-value hedge changes and hedged item gains/losses recognized in earnings; effective cash-flow hedge gains/losses recorded in other comprehensive income with ineffective portions in earnings; derivative cash flows included in operating activities.

nodes.title: Allowance for Funds Used During Construction
nodes.heading: Allowance for Funds Used During Construction
nodes.start_phrase: AFUDC is a non-cash credit to income with a corresponding charge to utility plant that represents the cost of borrowed funds or a return on equity funds devoted to plant under construction.
nodes.summary:
- Income taxes: Explains recognition of deferred income taxes for temporary differences using enacted rates, with regulated utility subsidiaries recording regulatory assets and liabilities for tax effects previously flowed through to customers. Investment tax credits are deferred and amortized over asset service lives. The company records interest and penalties in income tax expense and reports sales taxes on a net basis. Reference to Note 15—Income Taxes.

- Allowance for Funds Used During Construction (AFUDC): Describes AFUDC as a non-cash credit to income with a corresponding addition to utility plant, recorded as permitted by regulators. Borrowed-funds AFUDC reduces interest expense; equity-funds AFUDC is included in other, net. Reported amounts (in millions): other funds used during construction of $30 (2020), $28 (2019), $24 (2018); borrowed funds used during construction of $13 each year (2020–2018).

- Environmental costs: Outlines compliance with environmental regulations and the accounting for related costs—expensing or capitalizing current/future benefit expenditures and accruing remediation costs on an undiscounted basis when probable and estimable. Notes a conservation agreement with NOAA to protect steelhead trout in the Carmel River, requiring $1 million annual payments from 2010 through 2021. Remediation accruals were $1 million (2020) and $2 million (2019).

- Derivative financial instruments: States derivatives are used solely for hedging interest rate risk (no speculation or leverage), recognized at fair value, and may be designated as fair-value or cash-flow hedges. Details income statement treatment for fair-value and cash-flow hedges, with hedge cash flows included in operating activities. Reference to Note 12—Long-Term Debt.

nodes.title: Environmental Costs
nodes.heading: Environmental Costs
nodes.start_phrase: The Company’s water and wastewater operations and the operations of its Market-Based Businesses are subject to U.S. federal, state, local and foreign requirements relating to environmental protection, and as such, the Company periodically becomes subject to environmental claims in the normal course of business.
nodes.summary:

- Allowance for Funds Used During Construction (AFUDC): Describes AFUDC as a non-cash credit to income with a corresponding increase to utility plant; recorded as permitted by regulators; borrowed-funds AFUDC reduces interest expense, equity-funds AFUDC is in other, net; provides AFUDC amounts for 2018–2020.

- Derivative financial instruments: States derivatives are used solely to hedge interest rate exposure (no speculation or leverage); all derivatives recorded at fair value; permits fair-value hedge and cash-flow hedge designations; fair-value hedge gains/losses recognized in earnings along with hedged item; effective portions of cash-flow hedges recorded in other comprehensive income and reclassified when earnings are affected; any ineffectiveness recognized in earnings; derivative cash flows included in operating activities; references Note 12—Long-Term Debt.

nodes.title: Derivative Financial Instruments
nodes.heading: Derivative Financial Instruments
nodes.start_phrase: The Company uses derivative financial instruments for purposes of hedging exposures to fluctuations in interest rates.

  - Accounting for Convertible Instruments and Contracts in an Entity’s Own Equity: simplifies models for convertible instruments and EPS; effective 1/1/2022 with optional modified or full retrospective adoption; Company is evaluating impact and timing.

nodes.summary:
- Litigation update (Tennessee): The Tennessee-American Water Defendants sought dismissal for failure to state a claim and, for the parent company, lack of personal jurisdiction (filed Nov. 22, 2019; argued Sept. 9, 2020). On Sept. 24, 2020, at plaintiffs’ request, all claims against the parent company and the service company were dismissed without prejudice. The company believes TAWC has meritorious defenses and cannot estimate the likelihood or amount of loss.
- Carmel River diversion compliance and Monterey Peninsula Water Supply Project (Cal Am, California): Under SWRCB orders from 2009 and 2016, Cal Am must significantly reduce Carmel River diversions by Dec. 31, 2021.
